DEFENDANTS’ RULE 56.1 STATEMENT OF MATERIAL FACTS Pursuant to Eastern District of Louisiana Local Rule 56.1, Defendants LP Ind., LLC, CAG Holdings, LLC, RMH Holdings, Inc., Martian Sales, Inc., Johnson Foods, LLC, JOpen, LLC, Nuza, LLC, Calibre Manufacturing, LLC, FMK Group, Inc., PNW Holdings, LLC, CC US Holdings, LLC, Peyton Palaio, Mark Jennings, David Gabbay, and Mark Reilly (“Defendants”) respectfully submit this Statement of Material Facts in support of their Motion for Summary Judgment. I. HARMONY MOLLER 1. Harmony Moller died on February 6, 2023. ECF No. 100 at ¶ 30. 2. The Third Amended Complaint alleges that Ms. Moller, a 36-year-old female, died as the result of the ingestion of O.P.M.S. brand Kratom. Id. at ¶¶ 30, 33. 3. Plaintiff alleges that Harmony Moller consumed O.P.M.S. Silver Kratom ground leaf material sold as a loose powder or with the powder placed in a capsule. Ex. 1, MOLLER_000023; Ex. 2, MOLLER_000025.

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 23 4. Harmony was not feeling well and thought she had food poisoning immediately prior to her death. Ex. 3, STPSO000001 (the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office “Incident Report”), at 000001; Ex. 4, Excerpts from Deposition of Kathleen Moller (“Moller Dep.”) at 220:10, 225:4–10, Dec. 14, 2025; Ex. 5, ST.TAMMANYFD_MOLLER00001 (the St. Tammany Parish Fire Department EMS Records), at 00002. 5. Both O.P.M.S. Silver kratom powder products contained identical “directions” and “disclaimer” and “warning” labels. See Exs. 1, 2. 6. “A postmortem examination determined the cause of death was ‘Abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff exacerbated by Mitragynine use’ secondary to the ingestion of Kratom.” ECF No. 100 at ¶ 33. 7. Ms. Moller’s autopsy disclosed that she suffered from a coronary anomaly – specifically, her “left coronary artery arises 5 mm above the sinotubular ridge with an acute angle of origin[]” and “an inferior aortic wall flap[.]” Ex. 6, ST.TAMMANYCORONER_MOLLER00001 (St. Tammany Parish Coroner’s Office “STPCO” Records), at 00009, 00020–22. 8. All medical experts in this matter agree that Ms. Moller died of a ventricular arrhythmia. Ex. 7, Excerpts from Deposition of Dr. Allen Dollar (“Dollar Dep.”) at 87, Feb. 6, 2026; Ex. 8, Excerpts from Deposition of Dr. Winston Gandy (“Gandy Dep.”), at 71, Feb. 13, 2026; Ex. 9, Excerpts from Deposition of Dr. Josef Thundiyil (“Thundiyil Dep.”), at 151–52, Jan. 16, 2026; Ex. 10, Excerpts from Deposition of Dr. Amber Wang (“Wang Dep.”), at 98–99, Jan. 15, 2026; Ex. 11, Excerpts from Deposition of Dr. Ronald Wharton (“Wharton Dep.”), at 214:18– 215:16, Feb. 23, 2026; Ex. 12, Defendant’s Expert Report of Dr. Edward Boyer (“Boyer Rpt.”), at ¶ 79. 2

Limited postmortem toxicology testing was performed by NMS Labs, and testing was performed on femoral blood and vitreous blood (the “NMS Labs Test”).1 Ex. 13, Excerpts from NMSLabs Production, at NMS_MOLLER00004–40; Ex. 6 STPCO, at 00014–18; Ex. 14, Excerpts from Deposition of Dr. Michael DeFatta (“DeFatta Dep.”), at 144:4–11. 10. The NMS Labs Test did not quantify the amount of caffeine – it was only a presumptive positive. Id.; Ex. 14, DeFatta Dep. at 127:9–129:3, 144:4–11, 146:23–21; 188:10–24, 202:13–19, Feb. 25, 2026; Ex. 15, Excerpts from Deposition of Dr. Boyer Dep. (“Boyer Dep.”), at 253:2–7, Feb. 17, 2026. 11. The NMS Labs Test did not include testing to screen for food poisoning. Ex. 14, DeFatta Dep., at 117:24–118:11. 12. Mitragynine was detected at a concentration of 150 ng/mL. Ex. 6, STPCO, at 00014. 13. Other positive findings included diphenhydramine (64 ng/mL), promethazine (18 ng/mL), caffeine, and marijuana (delta-9 THC and delta-9 Carboxy THC). Id. 14. Diphenhydramine and promethazine have been scientifically proven to cause QT prolongation that can lead to a ventricular arrhythmia. Ex. 7, Dollar Dep. at 55:14–16, 69:1–5, 102:20–103:1. 15. Harmony Moller did not have a prescription for either Diphenhydramine or promethazine. Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) is a tropical tree native to Southeast Asia. Two alkaloids in kratom are mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, which interact with receptors in the brain. Ex. 12, Boyer Rpt., ¶¶ 20–21; Ex. 30, Expert Report of Marilyn Huestis, Ph.D., (“Huestis Rpt.”), ¶ 12; Ex. 31, Declaration of Jack E. Henningfield, Ph.D. (“Henningfield Decl.”), ¶ 13. 58. Kratom has been consumed for thousands of years in southeast Asia. Kratom was traditionally used in Southeast Asia for fatigue and to improve stamina (by laborers), pain relief, and for opium withdrawal. Ex. 33, Expert Report of Dennis Paustenbach, Ph.D., DABT, CIH 9

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 23 (“Paustenbach Rpt.”), ¶¶ 48, 114; Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl., ¶ 14. Kratom is typically consumed as crushed leaves, powder, extracts, capsules, liquids, or brewed into tea. Ex. 33, Paustenbach Rpt., ¶¶ 64, 95, 97, 112, 119. 59. In the U.S. and elsewhere, kratom is used to help with chronic pain, anxiety or depression, and opioid withdrawal or substitution. Id., ¶¶ 48, 68; Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl., ¶ 14. 60. Unlike opioids, Kratom does not produce respiratory depressant effects, nor carry opioid-like risks of death. Ex. 34, Expert Report of Jack Henningfield (“Henningfield Rpt.”), ¶ 49; Ex. 30, Huestis Rpt., ¶¶ 8–18; Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 15. 61. The product at issue here consists only of ground leaves from the tree – there is no other ingredient. Ex. 56, Excerpts from Nuza Dep. 34:5–7, Oct. 10, 2025. 62. These factual statements have been evaluated and verified as true by the Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”), the U.S. Assistant Secretary of Health, and the World Health Organization’s Expert Committee on Drug Dependence which conducted an initial review to determine if kratom warranted a full review as a potential path to international scheduling and determined that the evidence did not warrant such. Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 15; Ex. 34, Henningfield Rpt., ¶¶ 49–59, 78, 101–102. 63. Kratom is not an opioid or narcotic due to the nature of its botanical origin, its chemical structure, its known overall pharmacology, and the fact that it does not have the high abuse potential and national drug threat assessment necessary to meet statutory requirements for U.S. Controlled Substances Act (“CSA”) Scheduling or requirements for inclusion in the United Nations International Drug Control Treaties. Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 16. 64. Most people use kratom for health and well-being, including as a supplement to, or replacement for, caffeinated beverages and to self-manage depression, anxiety, pain, opioid and 10

The vast majority of the evidence from which the foregoing facts were obtained was generated by independent researchers primarily supported by the National Institutes of Health (“NIH”) and NIDA. Ex. 34, Henningfield Rpt., ¶¶ 102, 116–120; Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 20. These studies have been published at an increasing rate year by year over the past decade in leading biomedical research institutions, including Johns Hopkins, University of Florida, the NIDA intramural program itself, and many others. Ex. 34, Henningfield Rpt., ¶¶ 116–120; Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 20. 65. Kratom is a legally marketed and sold product in 43 states. Ex. 34, Henningfield Rpt., ¶¶ 109–113; Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 21. Several of the states that placed kratom as a Schedule I drug in their Controlled Substances Act between 2014 to 2016 are presently in the process of replacing those laws with laws to ensure legal access. Ex. 34, Henningfield Rpt., ¶ 112; Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 21. 66. Kratom is legally sold in the United States after Congress, the DEA, and the Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”)—the agency under which the FDA is organized—intensively investigated and deliberated about how to classify it. Ex. 34, Henningfield Rpt., ¶¶ 109–113; Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 22. The Secretary of HHS and Commissioner of the FDA have both testified before Congress that it is in the public health interest to keep kratom available for purchase over the counter. Ex. 31, Henningfield Decl. ¶ 22. They concluded that thousands of people would die from opioid overdoes if kratom was not made available as a substitute to opioids to the millions of people in the country who regularly purchase kratom. Id. 67. On August 21, 2014, the DEA requested that HHS conduct a medical and scientific evaluation of kratom to determine whether it should be recommended for scheduling as a controlled substance pursuant to the CSA. Id. ¶ 23. While HHS’s evaluation was ongoing, on 11

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 12 of 23 August 31, 2016, the DEA announced its intent to temporarily add kratom to Schedule I of the CSA.2 Id. In response, thousands of citizens submitted numerous formal comments providing compelling evidence and testimony that kratom is not harmful, but rather critical to healing, managing pain, and combating opiate and alcohol addiction.3 Id. These comments explained that kratom is safer than prescription opioids and that, compared to opioids, deaths attributable to kratom overdose are essentially non-existent. Id. 68. U.S. Representatives Mark Pocan (D-WI) and Matt Salmon (R-AZ) sent a letter to DEA and the Office of Management and Budget—a letter that received bipartisan support and was signed by 50 members of Congress—against any ban. Id. ¶ 24. The letter noted that kratom is an internationally consumed herb and condemned the proposed ban as “hasty” because of known beneficial effects of kratom. Id. The letter said that a ban would adversely affect consumer access to kratom’s known benefits and undermine innovative products that could be used to treat individuals suffering from addiction. Id. 69. A bipartisan group of U.S. Senators sent a generally similar letter to the DEA as the Representatives letter, making similar arguments about the adverse public health benefits of a Schedule I ban.4 The co-sponsors were Orrin G. Id. 73. In August 2018 the Assistant Secretary of Health, Dr. Brett Giroir charged with FDA scheduling recommendations to DEA, withdrew FDA’s 2017 scheduling recommendation to the DEA. In the formal scheduling recission letter, he stated that the “recission is based on many factors, in part on new data, and in part on the relative lack of evidence, combined with an unknown and potentially substantial risk to public health if these chemicals were scheduled at this time.” Id. ¶ 31.8 As a result, the DEA ceased its scheduling efforts. Id. This is the only time in United States’ history that the DEA has withdrawn a proposed scheduling. Id. 74. Since Dr. Giroir’s withdrawal letter, there have been several hundred new published research reports that further strengthen the case for kratom not being appropriate for scheduling. Id. ¶ 32. The DEA has not taken further action with respect to kratom. Id. 75. In December 2021, the Expert Committee on Drug Dependence (“ECDD”) at the World Health Organization and the U.S. Commission of Narcotic Drugs, comprised of 12 international experts on substance safety and addiction, unanimously concluded that there was insufficient evidence to recommend a critical international scheduling review of kratom. The FDA has not begun to promulgate or issue a proposed or final rule specific to the regulation of kratom and has only recently begun to conduct formal scientific studies of kratom. Id. ¶ 34. In January 2024, the FDA posted a new grant opportunity to fund the first clinical trial “to characterize the abuse potential and subjective effects of botanical Kratom.” Id.10 77. Recently, on September 19, 2024, the FDA issued preliminary results of its first study on kratom products, which showed clearly, as the agency put it, that “[k]ratom leaves appear safe even at high doses when taken in capsule form.” Id.11 ¶ 35. SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE AS OF FEBRUARY 2023 91. Kratom has not been shown to increase the risk of adverse cardiovascular effects in humans, nor pose significant cardiovascular risks from chronic use at any dose evaluated. Ex. 33, Paustenbach Rpt., ¶ 340; Ex. 37, Expert Report of Allen L. Dollar, MD, FACC, FACP, (“Dollar Rpt.”), ¶¶ 11, 22. 92. The concentration of mitragynine in Ms. Harmony Moller’s postmortem femoral blood (150 ng/mL) was within the range of mitragynine concentrations measured in healthy normal mitragynine users after a single 53.2 mg mitragynine dose—one not associated with toxicity. Ex. 30, Huestis Rpt., ¶ 28. 93. Scientific literature demonstrates that the postmortem concentration of mitragynine is approximately triple that of premortem measurements. Ex. 12, Boyer Rpt., ¶ 75. 94. At the time of Harmony Moller’s death in February 2023, published studies had assessed regular kratom users for evidence of cardiovascular toxicity through the performance of 18
